p: Léa hates Monday mornings. She hates the smell of the school corridor when the doors open: cheap perfume, new school bags and people pretending to be important.
She walks through the crowd with her bag against her chest. She has headphones in her ears. There is no music. But the headphones are her shield. Nobody talks to a person with headphones.
"Léa! Léaaaa!"
She pretends she does not hear. Two seconds. Three.
"Léa, I can see you!"
Inès appears next to her, out of breath. Her hair is perfect, even at eight o'clock in the morning. She gently pulls one headphone out of Léa's ear.
"You heard me. Admit it."
Léa smiles. It is the smile she wears every day, like a coat. Practical. Necessary. Not really hers.
"Hello, Inès."
"Did you hear? Madame Bertin cancelled the maths test! This day is starting well!" Inès puts her arm under Léa's arm.
Léa nods. She should be happy. She feels nothing.

They walk together to their classroom. Inès talks and talks. She talks about the party on Saturday, about the people who were there, about the people who should not be there. Léa listens. Or she pretends to listen. Now, for her, it is the same thing.
At her desk, Léa takes a small dark blue notebook out of the inside pocket of her bag. She opens it at the last page and reads, in silence, the lines she wrote last night:

*I smile, but I don't know why anymore.*
*I talk, but nobody hears my real voice.*
*Who am I when nobody is watching?*
She closes the notebook quickly when Inès turns around.
"What are you doing tonight? We're going to the shopping centre with the others."
Léa pushes the notebook to the bottom of her bag.
"Of course," she answers. With the smile she wears every day.
The shopping centre smells of fried food and expensive perfume. It is a strange mix, but Léa thinks it is honest. It is the world as it really is: beautiful on the outside, complicated inside.
There are four of them. Inès, Léa, and two girls from the popular group. Léa doesn't really know them. Camille is tall and blonde and laughs too loudly. Jade only talks while she looks at her phone.
"Did you see the new collection at Zara?" says Camille, and she pulls Inès towards the shop window.
Léa follows. Like always.

In the shop, Inès tries on a jacket. Léa stops in front of a mirror. She looks at her reflection. Hair tied back. Beige jumper. Classic jeans. Nothing different. Nothing surprising. Nothing that says *me*.
"Léa, what do you think?" asks Inès. She turns around with a red jacket on her shoulders.
"It looks great on you."
"You always say that."
"Because it's always true."
Inès laughs and looks back at the mirror, happy. Léa continues to look at her own reflection. The girl in the mirror. She knows her. But does she like her?
Later, they sit in a fast-food restaurant. Camille speaks in the voice of someone with important news.
"There's a party on Saturday at Thomas's house. Everybody's going. Are you coming?"
"Of course!" says Inès, looking at Léa.
Léa feels something tight in her chest. A party. People she hardly knows. Conversations she doesn't know how to have. Hours of smiling for no reason.
"Yes," she says anyway. "Sure."
Jade looks up from her phone for the first time that evening.
"Cool," she says. And she goes back to her screen.
On the way home, Inès puts her arm under Léa's, like always.
"I'm happy you're here, you know," she says softly. "You're my best friend."

Léa feels something warm in her chest. Inès really loves her. She is sure of that. But does Inès really know the Léa of the blue notebook? The Léa who writes poems at midnight? The Léa who is afraid of everything but dreams of everything?
"You're my best friend too," she answers.
And it is true. Just not complete.
That night, at home, she takes out her notebook and writes one line:
*You can love someone without that person really knowing you.*
She turns off the light and stays awake for a long time, her eyes open in the dark.
It is a Wednesday afternoon. Nothing special.

Léa didn't go to the party at Thomas's house. She said she had a headache. Inès was not happy, but she didn't insist. Now Léa is walking alone in the streets of the town centre, her hands in her pockets. She has no plan. No destination.
She likes walking alone. It is the only time when she doesn't have to smile for anybody.

She turns into a small street. She doesn't know it. The buildings are old but colourful, with flowers in the windows and art on the walls. At the end of the street, a bright yellow door catches her eye.
Above the door, there is a small handwritten sign:

WRITING WORKSHOP — OPEN TO EVERYONE
Wednesdays, 3 to 5 p.m. — Free entry
Léa stops.
Her heart does something strange. Not a strong beat. More like a little shiver. Like when you recognize someone.
She looks at the time on her phone. 3:12.
She looks at the yellow door.
She walks away.
Ten steps.
She stops.
She comes back.
The yellow door is still there, calm, without judgement.
*Free entry.* Two simple words. But for Léa, they mean something more. *Free.* The word rings somewhere inside her.
She pushes the door.

Inside, the room is small and warm. Tables in a circle. Papers everywhere. Books in every corner. A smell of coffee and old paper. Six or seven people of different ages are already sitting there. Nobody looks surprised. Nobody asks who she is.
A woman of about fifty, with grey hair and round glasses, simply looks up and smiles.
"Welcome. Take a chair. We start in five minutes."
Léa sits at the end of the table. Her back is straight. Her bag is on her knees. She is ready to leave at the first feeling of discomfort.
The woman with the round glasses claps her hands softly.
"For those who don't know me yet, my name is Marianne. Here, we write, we read, we share. No judgement, no competition. Just words, and people who love them."
She puts a white sheet of paper in the middle of the table.
"Today the subject is simple: write one thing you have never said out loud."
Léa's throat becomes tight.
She looks at the white paper in front of her. At the pen in her hand. And without thinking, without stopping herself for the first time in a long time, she writes:
*I don't know who I am. And I'm afraid nobody wants to know the answer.*
She puts down her pen. Her hands are shaking a little.
But something in her chest, for the first time in a long time, is breathing.
Marianne has a soft but confident voice. It is the voice of someone who learned to listen before speaking.

She goes around the table and asks each person if they want to read what they wrote. Some people read out loud with confidence. Others whisper shyly. A man of about forty laughs at his own sentence, and everybody laughs with him. Nobody is making fun of him.
When Marianne arrives in front of Léa, she simply looks at her.
"Do you want to share?"
Léa looks down at her paper. Two lines that say everything. The fear she has carried for so long.
"No," she says very quietly.
"That's perfect," says Marianne with a smile. "The important thing is that you wrote it."
She moves on to the next person. She doesn't insist. Léa feels something relax in her chest. Here, nobody forces her. Nobody expects her to be a special kind of person.
It is at this moment that she notices the two others.
On her left, a girl with short hair and rings on every finger is writing with total concentration. The tip of her tongue is between her teeth. She looks like she lives inside her own words.

Across the table, a boy with dark eyes and a quiet smile is drawing little pictures between his sentences. When he reads his text out loud — a short, funny story about a man who is afraid of his own reflection — a few people clap softly.
Léa claps too. She means it.
The boy meets her eyes and nods with a small smile. Not the kind of smile you wear to make a good impression. The kind of smile you can't stop.
At the end of the session, Marianne gives everyone a sheet with the next dates.
"We meet every Wednesday. The door is always open."
People stand up, talk a little, put away their things. Léa stays in her chair one second longer, her eyes on her paper. On the two sentences she wrote.
The girl with the rings stops next to her while she puts on her jacket.
"Is this your first time here?"
"Yes," says Léa.
"You can always see first times," says the girl. Her smile is kind. "You have that surprised look. Like you just found out you can breathe in a different way."
Léa doesn't know what to say. Because that is exactly it.
"I'm Sofia," says the girl, and she holds out her hand.
"Léa."
"Will you come back?"
Léa looks one last time at the yellow door. The piles of books. The round table. The white paper where she told the truth for the first time.
"Yes," she says. "I'll come back."
That evening at home, she doesn't write anything in her blue notebook. She lies on her bed, her eyes on the ceiling, and stays silent.
But this silence is different. It isn't empty.
It is full of something she can't name yet.
Something that looks like her.
The next Wednesday, Léa tells her mother she has an extra study hour at school.
It isn't completely a lie. She is learning something. Just not what her mother thinks.

The yellow door is waiting for her like an old friend. This time Léa pushes it without hesitating. No more ten steps back. No more shaking. Only that little familiar shiver in her chest, the one that says: *you belong here.*
Sofia is already there, in the same place, with a coffee in her hands. She looks up and smiles.
"You came back."
"I told you I would."
"People say a lot of things," says Sofia with a shrug. "But you're here. That's better."
The boy with the dark eyes arrives a few minutes later. He is a little out of breath, with his notebook under his arm. He sits across from Léa, like the first time.
"Adam," he says simply, and he holds out his hand.
"Léa."
"I know. Sofia told me about you."
Léa looks at Sofia, surprised. Sofia drinks her coffee innocently.
The session starts. Today's subject is *a place where you feel free*. Léa smiles inside. She doesn't need to think for long.

She writes for twenty minutes without looking up. Here the words come differently. No filter. No fear of judgement. She describes an imaginary bedroom. The walls are covered with pages torn from books. The window looks out on a sky that is always orange. Nobody ever knocks on the door.
This time, when Marianne stops in front of her, Léa hesitates for one second.
Then she reads.
At first her voice shakes a little. Then it becomes stronger, word after word, sentence after sentence. When she finishes, the silence lasts two seconds.
Sofia claps first. Adam follows, with a real smile. Marianne nods with that special expression of people who recognize something true.
"Beautiful writing," she says simply.
Two words. Léa carries them all week like a treasure.
On Friday evening, Inès calls her.
"Where were you on Wednesday? I tried to call you after school."
"At the library," says Léa. "Studying."
"Again? You don't need to study. You're already good at everything."
Léa laughs softly. It is the light laugh she uses to change the subject.
"And the party on Saturday?" asks Inès. "This time you're coming. I won't accept a headache."
"I'll be there," Léa promises.
She hangs up and stares into space. In one hand, her phone. In the other, her blue notebook.
Two worlds. Two Léas.
For now, the two worlds hold together. But deep inside, she knows it won't last.
Fragile balances always break in the end.
Three Wednesdays pass.
Léa doesn't miss one. She invents three different excuses. A study hour. A group project. An appointment at the dentist. Her mother doesn't ask many questions. Her father doesn't ask any.
At the workshop, something is slowly changing inside her. Like a plant that finally gets water after a long dry season.

Sofia is the kind of person who takes up all the space without noticing. Not because she is arrogant. Just because she exists. She talks loudly and laughs even more loudly. And she looks at people as if she really wants to find what is behind their eyes.
One Wednesday after the session, she and Léa sit on the windowsill with two coffees from the machine in the corridor. Sofia opens her notebook at a page full of crossed-out words.
"Listen to this and tell me if it's bad," she says.
She reads a short text about her grandmother, who used to sing in the kitchen. It is simple, precise, alive. Léa feels her throat become tight.
"It isn't bad at all," she says.
"You almost cried."
"No."
"Your eyes were shining."
"It's the coffee," says Léa.
Sofia laughs. A real laugh, from the stomach.
"I like how bad you are at lying," she says.
Léa smiles. A real smile this time. Not the coat. Something more fragile and more honest.

Adam is different. He is quieter than Sofia, with the calm presence of people who watch a lot before they speak. He writes short stories with unexpected endings. Often funny, sometimes sad, always surprising.
One evening he shows Léa one of his stories on his phone. It is about a boy who collects the ends of days, because he is afraid of tomorrow.
"Is it about you?" asks Léa.
"A little," he admits. "Writing is always a little bit about yourself, isn't it?"
Léa thinks of her blue notebook. Of all the sentences she wrote in the dark.
"Yes," she says. "I think so."
There is a comfortable silence between them. The kind of silence you don't try to fill.
"You have a special style, you know," says Adam, without looking at her. "When you read your texts, you can feel that every word was chosen. Not arranged. Chosen."
Léa doesn't answer immediately. Because nobody has ever said something like that to her. Not about her writing. Not about her.
"Thank you," she says at last.
"It isn't a compliment," he says. "It's just true."

That night at home, Léa takes out her blue notebook and writes for a long time. She writes about Sofia and Adam. About Marianne and the yellow door. About how it feels to be seen by people who don't expect anything from her.
At the end, she writes this:

*Some people look at you and see what you should be.*
*And some people look at you and see what you already are.*
*The second kind is rare. When you find them, you must keep them.*
She reads it twice.
Then she draws a circle around it.
November arrives with its short days and heavy skies.
Léa is juggling. Every week it is a little more difficult.

On Wednesdays at the workshop, she is the Léa who writes, who laughs with Sofia, who talks honestly with Adam. The rest of the time, she is the other Léa. The one who smiles in the corridors, who goes to parties she doesn't want to go to, who gives good answers in class so she doesn't disappoint her parents.
Two lives. One body. One head.
And the head is getting tired.
One Thursday morning, Inès is waiting in front of the classroom. She has the face she makes when something is worrying her.
"Where were you last night? I called you four times."
"My phone was on silent," says Léa.
"The library again?"
"Yes."
Inès looks at her for one second too long.
"Léa, you've been strange for three weeks."
"I'm not strange."
"You're distant. You're always in your head. Even when you're here, you're not really here."

Léa feels something tighten in her chest. Inès is not wrong. But how can she explain? How can she say *I'm living something that finally feels like me* without hurting someone who already thinks she knows her?
"Everything's fine," she says. "I just have a lot of work right now."
Inès nods slowly. She isn't completely convinced.
"OK," she says. "But you're my best friend. If something is happening, you can tell me."
"I know," says Léa.
She smiles. The coat.
Inès smiles back. And Léa hates this moment. Because Inès deserves better than a fake smile.
On Friday evening, her mother calls her from the kitchen while she is going up to her room.
"Léa, did you get your school report?"
"Not yet," she answers from the stairs.
"Madame Bertin sent me a message. She says you seem less focused in class these last few weeks."
Léa stops on the stairs.
"I'm focused."
"She says you're not."
"Madame Bertin likes to make a drama out of everything."
Her mother appears at the bottom of the stairs. Her arms are crossed. She has the look she uses when she wants a real answer.
"What's going on, Léa?"
"Nothing, Mum. Everything's fine."
"Are you sure?"
"Completely."
Her mother looks at her for one more second, then goes back into the kitchen. Léa goes up to her room, closes the door and sits on her bed.
Her phone vibrates. A message from Sofia.
*Are you writing something for Wednesday? Marianne wants a longer text this week.*
Léa looks at the message. Then at her bedroom door. Then at the blue notebook on her desk.
She answers: *Yes. I already have an idea.*
It is true. But the idea scares her. Because the text she wants to write is about a girl who lives two lives and doesn't know which one is real anymore.
Too close to the truth.
Or maybe that is exactly why.
She opens her notebook and starts to write.
Outside, the wind is hitting the window.
The cracks are getting bigger.
That Wednesday, the session is special.

Marianne asked for a longer text. Léa wrote six pages. Six pages about a girl between two worlds, two faces, two versions of herself. She read it in front of everybody. This time her voice was firm. It didn't shake.
When she finished, the silence lasted longer than usual. Sofia put her hand on Léa's arm without a word. Adam was looking at his paper, but his eyes were shining. Marianne simply said:
"That's your best text."
Léa goes home that evening with something light in her chest. Almost happiness. The real kind.
She shouldn't put her bag down in the hall so quickly.
Her mother is sitting at the kitchen table. Straight. Hands together. The blue notebook is on the table in front of her.
Léa stops.
The world stops.
"Mum... that notebook..."
"I was tidying your room," says her mother in a flat voice. "It was under your mattress."
"You had no right to..."
"I read it," says her mother. "All of it."
Léa feels something break inside her. That notebook is her most secret place. Her truest fears. Her most fragile dreams. Her deepest doubts. Words written for nobody. Words written only for herself.
"It's private," she says. Her voice is shaking.
"You've been lying for weeks. The library, the study hours... You go to a writing workshop? You spend your time writing poems?"
"It's not..."
"Léa, you have your final exams to prepare!"
"I know!"
"So why are you wasting your time with this nonsense?"
The word falls like a stone.
*Nonsense.*
Everything she wrote. Everything she felt. Everything she built in this notebook for years. Nonsense.
Something wakes up inside her. Something she has never let out.
"It isn't nonsense," she says.
Her mother opens her mouth, but Léa continues. The words are coming out now, and she can't stop them.
"It's the only thing that really belongs to me. The only place where I'm me. Not the good girl everybody wants me to be. Not the good student. Not the perfect best friend. Me. Just me."
"You don't even know what I like, Mum. You never asked me. You ask about my grades. You ask if I ate well. You ask if I studied. But you never ask what I really feel."
Her mother stands up. Her face is closed, but something in her eyes is moving.
"I do all this for you. Everything I do is so that you have a better life than mine."
"I don't want your life, Mum. I want mine."
The silence after that is different from other silences. Heavier. Fuller. Like the air before a storm.
Her father appears in the doorway. He heard the voices. He looks at his wife, then at his daughter. And, like always, he says nothing.
That silence hurts even more than her mother's words.
Léa takes her notebook from the table. She holds it tight against her chest.
"This notebook isn't nonsense," she says one last time. "It's me."
She goes up to her room and closes the door softly. No slamming. No more shouting. Just a soft close that says: *I said what I had to say.*
She sits on her bed in the dark. The notebook against her chest. Her heart beating fast.
She waits for the tears. They don't come.
Instead, there is something else. Something new.
A small flame. Fragile, but real.
She spoke. For the first time in her life, she said the truth out loud. Not in a notebook. Not on a white sheet of paper at the workshop.
To her mother. Face to face.
And the world didn't fall apart.
In the dark, she opens her notebook and writes one sentence without seeing:
*Today I existed out loud.*
The next morning, nobody talks at breakfast.
Her mother puts the bowl of coffee in front of her without a word. Her father reads his newspaper with very suspicious concentration. Léa eats quickly and leaves for school without saying goodbye.
In the street, the cold air feels good. She walks faster than usual, as if she can run away from the bad feeling that has followed her since last night.
At school, Inès meets her at the gate.
"Are you OK? You look..."
"I didn't sleep well," says Léa. "That's all."
Inès looks at her but doesn't insist. They go in together, in silence. A heavy silence that is new between them.

In class, Léa hears almost nothing. The teachers' voices come from far away, like under water. She thinks about her mother's face last night. About her own words. About the fragile flame she felt inside.
Was she right to speak?
Did she ruin everything?
The next Wednesday, she doesn't get up to go to the workshop.
She lies on her bed and looks at the ceiling. At 3:05, a message from Sofia appears on her phone.
*Where are you? The session has started.*
She doesn't answer.
At 3:30, Adam writes too.
*Is everything OK?*
She puts the phone face down on the mattress.
The yellow door is waiting for her somewhere in town. Marianne. Sofia. Adam. The white sheets of paper. The true words. Everything that looks like her.

But something is too heavy today. The fight with her mother. Her father's silence. The way Inès looks at her, knowing she is hiding something. The feeling that she pulled every thread at the same time and now everything is coming apart.
She opens her notebook. She closes it without writing.
It is the first time the words don't come.
Her mother knocks on her door at the end of the afternoon.
"Léa?"
"Yes."
"Dinner's ready."
A silence.
"Mum?"
"Yes."
"I... nothing. I'm coming."

She hears her mother's steps going away down the corridor. She almost said something. What exactly, she doesn't know. Maybe *I'm sorry.* Maybe *I love you too, even if we don't understand each other.* Maybe just *I'm here.*
But the words got stuck somewhere between her throat and her mouth.
Dinner happens in a polite, painful silence. Her father talks about the weather. Her mother serves the plates. Léa eats without tasting anything.
Before going to bed, she walks past her parents' room. The door is half open. She hears her father's low voice.
"We have to give her time, Nadia."
And her mother's voice, more tired than angry.
"I just want her to be happy. That's all I want."
Léa stands very still in the corridor.
She didn't imagine this. Her mother wants her to be happy but doesn't know how to show it. Her father understands in silence but doesn't know how to help.
Three people in the same house. Three lonely hearts that pass close to each other but never touch.
She goes back to her room. She sits at her desk. She takes her notebook.
This time the words come. Slowly at first. Then faster.

*You can hurt the people you love without wanting to.*
*You can be hurt by the people who love you without them knowing.*
*The distance between two hearts is not always a question of will.*
*Sometimes it's just a question of words we haven't found yet.*
She puts down her pen.
Outside, the night is calm.
But inside her, something is still searching. Searching for the way. Searching for the words. Searching for how to be herself without losing the people she loves.
She doesn't have the answer yet.
But for the first time, she knows she is really looking for it.
Two weeks pass.
Two weeks without the workshop. Without Sofia. Without Adam. Without the yellow door.

Léa still goes to school, eats, sleeps, answers when people talk to her. From the outside, everything looks normal. From the inside, it is like walking in cotton. Everything is soft. Everything is far away.
Inès notices first.
One Tuesday at lunch in the canteen, she puts her tray down in front of Léa and looks straight at her.
"Stop."
"Stop what?"
"Pretending everything's fine. You haven't been here for two weeks. Your body is here. But you — the real you — you're not here."
Léa opens her mouth to put on the usual coat. *Everything's fine. I'm just tired. It's the exams.*
But the words don't come.
Inès waits.
"I feel like I broke everything," Léa says at last. "My mum. You. The place where I was happy. I broke everything just because I wanted to be me."
Inès doesn't answer immediately. She takes some rice on her fork, then puts it down.
"You didn't break everything," she says softly. "But you could have talked to me, you know."
"I was afraid you wouldn't understand."
"Maybe I wouldn't understand everything. But I would try. That's what friends are for, right?"
Léa feels something loosen in her throat.
"I'm sorry, Inès."
"Stop saying sorry and tell me what's really going on."
So Léa talks. For the first time, she really talks to Inès. About the workshop. The blue notebook. Sofia and Adam. The fight with her mother. The feeling of being two different people in one body.
Inès listens without interrupting. Without taking out her phone. Without looking away.
When Léa finishes, Inès is quiet for a moment.
"Why did you never show me your poems?"
"Because I was scared."
"Of what?"
"That you'd think they were bad. That you'd look at me differently."
Inès shakes her head slowly.
"Léa. We've known each other since we were eleven. You could show me anything."
Léa looks at her tray. A tear falls without warning. She doesn't wipe it away immediately.
"I know," she says. "I think I was mostly scared that they were good. Because if they were good, I would have no excuse not to really do it."
Inès looks at her like someone who has just understood something important.
"You're really complicated, you know."
Léa laughs. A real laugh, wet with tears.
"I know."

That evening at home, Léa goes straight up to her room. She sits on the floor with her back against the bed and takes out her blue notebook. She turns the pages slowly from the beginning. Each page is a version of herself. Each sentence is a truth she only told this notebook.
She stops at the very first sentence she ever wrote in it. She was fourteen.
*I want to know who I am before other people tell me.*
She reads it three times.
That fourteen-year-old girl already knew. She knew what she needed. She was just afraid for two years.
She turns the pages to the last sentence she wrote.
*You can hurt the people you love without wanting to.*
Between these two sentences, there are two years of doubts, of gentle lies, of smiles worn like coats, of words written in the dark.
But there is also the workshop. Sofia. Adam. Marianne. The yellow door. The white sheets of paper. The voice that became stronger, word after word.
She takes her pen and writes under the last sentence:
*I think I've hit rock bottom. But that's what the bottom is for. You push against it to come back up.*
She closes the notebook.
Outside, it is starting to rain.
She takes her phone and writes a message to Sofia.
*I'm sorry about these two weeks. Is the yellow door still open for me?*
The answer arrives thirty seconds later.
*It was never closed. Wednesday, 3 p.m. Be there.*
Léa puts the phone on her desk.
For the first time in two weeks, she feels something warm in her chest.
Not happiness yet. Something smaller and stronger.
Hope.
Wednesday arrives with a blue sky, unusual for the season.

Léa gets up early. She takes a long shower and dresses with care — not to please anybody, just to feel good in her own skin. She takes her blue notebook and puts it in her bag. Not to hide it. To bring it with her.
In the kitchen, her mother is making coffee. They haven't really talked since the fight. Polite words. Practical questions. Nothing real.
Léa stops in the doorway.
"Mum."
Her mother turns around.
"I'm going to the writing workshop this afternoon. I'll be home around six."
It isn't a question. It isn't an excuse. It is just information, said clearly, eyes in eyes.
Her mother looks at her for a long second. Something crosses her face. Surprise. Resistance. And then something else. Something softer.
"OK," she says. "Be careful."
Two simple words. Not total approval. Not a complete reconciliation. But a door that is half open.
Léa nods.
"Thanks, Mum."
She goes out into the blue morning with something new in her step.
The yellow door is there, like always. Faithful, and without judgement.
Sofia is standing in the doorway with a coffee in her hand, as if she is waiting for her. She probably is.
"There you are," she says simply.
"Here I am," says Léa.
They go in together.
Adam looks up from his usual place and smiles. That quiet smile that promises nothing but gives a lot. Marianne nods from the back of the room.
Léa sits down. She takes out her blue notebook. She puts it on the table in front of her.
Marianne claps her hands softly.

"Today I want to try something different. No subject. Each of you will look through what you have already written and choose the text that is most *you*. The one you maybe never wanted to show. The one that is a little bit scary."
Léa looks down at her blue notebook.
*The one that is a little bit scary.*
She turns the pages slowly. Past the first poems, clumsy and searching. Past the sentences written in the dark after difficult nights. Past the pages that are creased from being read too many times.

She stops at a text she wrote three months ago, on a night when she couldn't sleep. Six short paragraphs about a girl who learned to be invisible to survive in a world that always asked her to be someone else.
It is the truest text she has ever written.
And the most terrifying.
The others read their texts one by one. Léa only half listens. Her heart beats harder and harder as her turn comes closer.
When Marianne looks at her, she knows it is time.
She opens her notebook at the right page. She takes a breath.
And she reads.

Her voice doesn't shake. It is clear and calm, and it carries every word with the care of someone who knows exactly what she is saying. She reads all six paragraphs to the end without stopping, without looking at the others, her eyes on her own writing, as if she is really reading herself for the first time.
When she finishes, she looks up.

Sofia's eyes are shining. Adam is looking at the table, but his jaw is tight, the way it is when something really touches him. A woman of about forty, whom Léa hardly knows, quietly wipes something under her eye.
Marianne looks at her for a long time.
"Léa," she says. "That voice. It's yours. Never lose it again."
The silence that follows is the most beautiful silence Léa has ever known.
Not the empty silence of dinners without conversation. Not the heavy silence of fights that aren't finished. Not the hollow silence of smiles worn like coats.
A full silence. A silence that is still listening.
She closes her notebook gently.
And for the first time in a very long time, she isn't trying to be someone else.
She is here. Whole. Present.
She is herself.
The next morning, Léa wakes up differently.
Nothing spectacular. No sudden light, no big revelation. Just a quiet feeling of living in her own body without saying sorry for being there.
She goes down to the kitchen. Her mother is already there with her coffee and her glasses on her nose. There is a magazine open in front of her, but she probably isn't reading it.
Léa sits down across from her.
"Mum. Can I read you something?"
Her mother looks up. Surprised. Careful.
"What is it?"
"A text I wrote. Not so that you change your mind about anything. Just so that you really know me."
A long silence.
Her mother takes off her glasses. She puts them on the table. She puts her hands together.
"I'm listening."
Léa takes out her blue notebook. She opens it at the text she read yesterday at the workshop. The scary one. The truest one.
And she reads.
Her voice is calm. Steady. No drama. Just the words and what they carry.
Her mother doesn't interrupt her once.
When Léa finishes, she closes the notebook and waits. Her heart is beating, but her hands are steady.
Her mother stays silent for a long moment. She is looking at the table. Something is moving on her face. Feelings looking for a way to the surface.
"I didn't know you felt invisible," she says at last. Her voice is different. Lower. More real.
"You couldn't know. I never told you."
"I should have asked."
"I should have answered honestly."
Her mother looks up. Her eyes are shining a little.
"You write well," she says. "Really well."
It is not much. But from her mother, it is huge.
"Thank you, Mum."
Her mother stands up, walks around the table and puts her hand on Léa's shoulder. It is a clumsy gesture. The gesture of someone who isn't used to showing tenderness, but who is trying anyway.
Léa puts her hand on her mother's hand.
They stay like that for one second. Two. Without speaking.
It isn't a perfect reconciliation. There will still be misunderstandings, difficult silences, disagreements. They are too different for everything to be fixed in one morning.
But it is a beginning. A real beginning.
A fragile bridge between two sides of a river.

On Saturday afternoon, Léa meets Inès in the park near school. They walk for a long time with no destination, hands in their pockets, like they did when they were eleven and the world seemed huge and full of possibilities.
"Can I show you something?" says Léa.
She takes out her blue notebook and opens it at a page in the middle. It is a short poem she wrote last year, about friendship and the fear of being really seen.
Inès reads it slowly. She reads it again.
"Is it about us?" she asks.
"A little. Mostly about me. About what I was afraid to show you."
Inès gives the notebook back carefully, as if it is something precious.
"It's beautiful, Léa. Really beautiful."
"You don't have to say that."
"I never say things just to be nice. You know that."
It's true. It is one of the things Léa loves most about Inès.
They keep walking. The low November sun draws long shadows on the path.
"You should have trusted me before," says Inès softly. There is no blame in her voice. It is just a fact.
"I know. I was afraid you'd look at me differently."
"I look at you differently now."
Léa stops.
"In a better way," Inès explains with a smile. "I see someone I didn't completely know. And I like what I see."
Léa feels something warm spread in her chest.
"I like you too," she says.
Inès puts her arm under Léa's arm, like always. But this time Léa isn't wearing the coat. She is just there. Herself. Whole.
And that is enough.
In the evening, in her room, she opens her blue notebook at a new white page. She thinks for a long time before writing.
Then she simply writes:

*Today I built two bridges.*
*They are still fragile. But they hold.*
*And I think I'm the one who built them.*
She smiles at the sentence.
Outside, the night is mild for the season.
Tomorrow there will still be problems. Misunderstandings. Days when being herself will cost something.
But tonight, Léa knows something she didn't know three months ago.
She knows she exists. Really. Completely.
And that this life is worth defending.
December arrives with its first frost and its lights in the windows.

Marianne announced something special for the last session before the holidays. A reading evening, open to the public. Everyone can invite anyone they want. Everyone will read a text of their choice in front of everybody.
Léa said yes immediately.
Then she spent three nights regretting it.

On the evening of the reading, she dresses with care. Not the usual beige jumper. A dark red dress she never dared to wear. She bought it one day without thinking and left it at the back of her wardrobe for six months. She ties her hair differently. She looks in the mirror.
The girl in the mirror looks like her.
Really, at last.
Downstairs, her mother is waiting in the hall with the car keys in her hand.
"I'll drive you," she says simply.
Léa looks at her, surprised.
"It's not far, I can walk..."
"I know. I'll drive you anyway."

In the car, they don't talk much. The radio is playing softly. The streets go past behind the windows. But this silence is different from all the other silences they have shared. It is peaceful. Almost like they are on the same team.
In front of the yellow door, her mother stops. She looks at the building for a moment.
"Is it here?"
"Yes."
Her mother nods slowly. As if she is trying to understand what this place means for her daughter. As if she is making a real, honest effort to see the world through Léa's eyes.
"Have a good evening," she says at last.
"Thank you, Mum. For everything."
Her mother smiles. A small, clumsy smile. But an honest one.
Léa gets out of the car and pushes the yellow door.
The room is transformed.
Marianne has put candles on the tables and extra chairs in a half circle. About twenty people are already there. Faces from the workshop, and new faces brought by everyone.
Sofia runs to her.
"You look amazing tonight."
"It's the red dress."
"It's you," says Sofia. "The red dress is just lucky."
Adam arrives behind her, hands in his pockets, with that quiet smile.
"Ready?"
"No," says Léa honestly.
"Perfect. The best texts come from there."
Inès is sitting in the third row, next to an empty chair with a bag on it to keep the place. She waves at Léa. Léa smiles at her. A real smile. Her own smile.
The evening begins.

One after another, the members of the workshop read their texts. Funny stories, sad poems, pieces of life put into words so precisely that they touch your heart. The audience really listens. It is the careful, respectful silence of people who understand that shared words are gifts.
When it is Léa's turn, Marianne says her name softly.
Léa stands up.
She walks to the small desk at the front of the room.
She looks at the faces in front of her. Inès in the third row. Sofia on the side. Adam, nodding very slightly. Marianne at the back, with her calm, confident smile.
And in the last row, standing against the wall: her father.
Léa stops.

Her father is here. He must have parked the car after her mother dropped her off. He must have found the address by himself. He is standing against the back wall with his coat still buttoned, like someone who isn't sure he is allowed to be there.
Their eyes meet.
He doesn't smile. He just nods, once. That simple gesture means: *I'm here. I see you. You can go.*

Léa feels something break softly in her chest. Not sadness. Something more complicated and more beautiful. The sudden understanding that the people we love sometimes surprise us at exactly the right moment.
She takes a breath.
She opens her blue notebook at the last page she wrote.
And she reads.

There is a girl I know well.
She smiles with other people's smiles.
She speaks with the words people expect.
She lives in the spaces between what others want.

One day she pushed a yellow door.
And on the other side there were white pages,
and people who wrote to be true.
And she understood that truth has a shape.
That this shape is words.
And that these words are her.

Today I recognize this girl.
In the mirror in the morning.
In the silences she doesn't try to fill anymore.
In the smiles she doesn't wear like coats anymore.

Her name is Léa.
She is sixteen.
And she is only beginning.
The silence after that lasts a long time.

Then the applause begins. Soft at first. Then louder. Sofia puts two fingers in her mouth and whistles. Inès claps and laughs, her eyes shining. Marianne puts her hands together with the face of someone who has just seen something rare.
And at the back of the room, her father is clapping too. Still standing against his wall. Still with his coat buttoned.
But his eyes are shining.
Léa closes her blue notebook.
She steps down.
She crosses the room to her father.
He opens his arms, a little clumsily. She steps into them. He holds her tight. Not for long. Just long enough.
"Well done," he whispers into her hair.
It isn't much. It is enough. It is him.

Later in the evening, while everyone is talking and laughing and sharing over a glass of orange juice, Léa sits alone in a corner for a moment. She takes out her blue notebook. She holds it in her hands.
This little notebook that kept everything. All her fears. All her doubts. All her truths whispered in the dark.
She opens it at the very first page. The sentence she wrote at fourteen.
*I want to know who I am before other people tell me.*
She smiles.
Then she turns to the last page. She takes her pen.
And she writes the last sentence of this chapter of her life.
*I think I know now.*
She closes the notebook.
Sofia comes over with two glasses.
"What are you thinking about?"
"Nothing," says Léa. "For the first time in a long time, absolutely nothing."
Sofia raises her glass.
"That's the best place to be."
Léa raises hers.
Outside, the December night is cold and full of stars.
And Léa — sixteen years old, blue notebook in her bag, red dress, a smile that belongs only to her — is exactly where she should be.
— The End —

title: Between Two Léas
author: Aude Lago Gbokoya
desc: Léa porte son sourire comme un manteau. Derrière une porte jaune, elle va trouver sa vraie voix. Le roman d'Aude.
